Before you learn a tool, you need to know the job the tool does. dbt lives inside a bigger world: companies collect data in many applications, copy it into a central warehouse, clean it, and then people use it to make decisions. dbt does one part of that work, and does it very well.

Many exam questions are not about syntax. They describe a situation ("the data team loads raw tables every hour", "a dashboard depends on this model", "the table has one row per order line") and ask what you should do. If you do not understand the words
, you will lose points even if you know dbt commands perfectly. This chapter gives you that vocabulary in simple words, using the practice data you will use in the whole book.

Companies copy raw data from their applications into a data warehouse, and then transform it there into clean, trustworthy tables that people can use. dbt is the tool that manages that transformation step, using SQL

statements organised like a software project. To do this well you must think in tables with a clear grain, split into facts and dimensions, and apply engineering habits like version control, testing and documentation.

Think of dbt as the head chef's recipe book plus a kitchen planner. The ingredients (raw data) are already in the fridge (the warehouse). The recipes (your SQL models) say how to prepare each dish. dbt reads all the recipes, figures out that the sauce must be ready before the pasta, and tells the kitchen staff (the warehouse engine) what to cook and in which order. dbt itself never stores any food.
dbt stores no data. All tables live in your warehouse.
It does not copy data from APIs or applications.
It produces the clean tables that dashboards read.
dbt makes SQL modular, testable and documented; the real work is still SQL running in the warehouse.
